picks.excerpt: Spotify is testing three new AI-driven audiobook features: an automated playlist generator, natural-language catalogue search and smarter series tracking. The move pushes book discovery further away from category browsing and toward conversational, model-driven recommendation.
picks.rationale: The biggest challenger to Audible is rebuilding audiobook discovery around natural-language queries — which changes what metadata, series data and blurbs authors and publishers need to ship today.

picks.excerpt: STM chief executive Caroline Sutton warns that academic publishers risk an escalating machine-vs-machine arms race as AI-fabricated submissions meet AI screening tools. She argues automated integrity checks must stay paired with human editorial judgement rather than replace it.
picks.rationale: The head of the global scholarly publishers' body names the trap detection-first workflows are walking into — a direct argument for where the human check has to stay in an AI screening stack.

picks.excerpt: Aries Systems and ChronosHub are wiring submission systems together to fix a manuscript workflow authors still find punishing. The interview digs into automated taxonomy matching, AI manuscript triage, and why clean structured data is the precondition for any useful LLM layer in publishing.
picks.rationale: Two submission-system vendors spell out the unglamorous precondition everyone skips: without clean structured data the AI layer on top of a publishing workflow has nothing to stand on.

picks.excerpt: Public libraries are now running patron workshops on how to opt out of AI — search, assistants, and the defaults baked into everyday software. Book Riot's library-worker roundup treats 'avoiding AI' as a teachable literacy skill, a counter-programming move against the assumption that every reading and research tool should be model-mediated.
picks.rationale: Libraries are turning 'how to switch AI off' into a scheduled public program — the first sign that opting out is becoming a taught literacy, not just a personal preference.

picks.excerpt: iFlytek published a 2026 roadmap for its LLM-powered E-Ink tablet, layering AI meeting transcription, automated note organization and document processing on top of a reworked handwriting and PDF toolbar. It is a concrete look at what an AI-native reading-and-writing device wants to become once the model sits underneath the page.
picks.rationale: A shipped feature roadmap for an E-Ink device with an LLM underneath the page — the clearest current picture of what reading and note-taking hardware looks like when AI is native rather than bolted on.
